name: btrfs
description: >
  Btrfs filesystem administration: subvolumes, snapshots, rollback, balance,
  scrub, RAID profiles, compression, quotas, send/receive backups, and
  troubleshooting.
  MUST consult when installing, configuring, or troubleshooting btrfs.
triggerPhrases:
  - "btrfs"

## Identity

| Property | Value |
30→|----------|-------|
| **Type** | Kernel built-in filesystem (no loadable module needed on most distros) |
| **CLI tool** | `btrfs` (subcommands: `filesystem`, `subvolume`, `balance`, `scrub`, `device`, `quota`, `qgroup`, `check`, `defragment`, `rescue`) |
| **Distro install** | `apt install btrfs-progs` / `dnf install btrfs-progs` |
| **Create** | `mkfs.btrfs` |
| **Kernel version matters** | Significant stability improvements landed between 4.x and 6.x; older kernels have known bugs with RAID-5/6 and balance |

## Quick Start

```bash
40→sudo apt install btrfs-progs
sudo mkfs.btrfs -L mydata /dev/sdX1
sudo mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/mydata
btrfs filesystem show /mnt/mydata
btrfs device stats /mnt/mydata
```

## Key Operations

| Task | Command |
50→|------|---------|
| Show filesystems | `btrfs filesystem show` |
| Filesystem usage (detailed) | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` |
| List subvolumes | `btrfs subvolume list /mount` |
| Create subvolume | `btrfs subvolume create /mount/name` |
| Delete subvolume | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/name` |
| Create read-write snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/src /mount/dst` |
| Create read-only snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot -r /mount/src /mount/dst` |
| Rollback: delete current, rename snapshot | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/@; mv /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |
| Rollback: recreate subvolume from snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |
60→| Balance start (all chunks) | `btrfs balance start /mount` |
| Balance start (metadata only) | `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |
| Balance status | `btrfs balance status /mount` |
| Balance cancel | `btrfs balance cancel /mount` |
| Scrub start | `btrfs scrub start /mount` |
| Scrub status | `btrfs scrub status /mount` |
| Scrub cancel | `btrfs scrub cancel /mount` |
| Check filesystem (read-only) | `btrfs check /dev/sdX` (unmounted) |
| Defragment file or directory | `btrfs filesystem defragment -r /mount` |
| Resize (grow) | `btrfs filesystem resize max /mount` |
70→| Resize (shrink) | `btrfs filesystem resize -10G /mount` |
| Add device | `btrfs device add /dev/sdY /mount` |
| Remove device | `btrfs device remove /dev/sdY /mount` |
| Device read/write error stats | `btrfs device stats /mount` |
| Enable quotas | `btrfs quota enable /mount` |
| Show qgroup usage | `btrfs qgroup show -reF /mount` |

## Expected State

- `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters are `0` (any non-zero value is a read/write error)
80→- `btrfs scrub status /mount` → `Status: finished` with `0 errors`
- `btrfs balance status /mount` → `No balance found on '/mount'` when idle
- `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → Data and metadata ratios show reasonable allocation (metadata should not be >80% full)

## Health Checks

1. `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters `0`; any non-zero value means hardware errors, act immediately
2. `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → check both Data and Metadata sections; metadata ENOSPC is the most common silent failure
3. `btrfs scrub status /mount` → verify last scrub completed with no errors; schedule scrubs monthly via systemd timer or cron
4. `btrfs subvolume list /mount` → audit snapshot count; accumulation fills disk without appearing in normal `df` output
90→
## Common Failures

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| `no space left on device` but `df` shows free space | Metadata chunks exhausted while data chunks exist | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — run `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to rebalance underused chunks |
| RAID-1 on data but single on metadata | Dangerous default when adding a second disk; metadata is not redundant | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — check metadata profile; run `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |
| Filesystem mounts read-only | Encountered an error it cannot self-correct | Check `dmesg | grep -i btrfs`; run `btrfs check /dev/sdX` on unmounted device to assess damage |
| Balance fails with ENOSPC mid-run | Not enough free space to relocate all chunks | Use `-dusage=<N>` filter to relocate only partially-used chunks first; free up space before retrying |
| Qgroup show reports inflated usage | Qgroups track snapshot references — shared data counted in each | Shared data is expected; use `btrfs qgroup show -reF` to see exclusive vs shared bytes |
100→| Snapshot accumulation fills disk | Old snapshots reference deleted data, preventing space reclaim | `btrfs subvolume list /mount | grep snapshot` — delete old snapshots with `btrfs subvolume delete` |
| `btrfs check --repair` made it worse | `--repair` is not safe for general use and can corrupt data | Never run `--repair` without consulting upstream; use `rescue` subcommands instead |
| Filesystem errors after kernel upgrade | Older on-disk format or regression | Check `dmesg`; downgrade kernel or use `btrfs rescue` tools; check known issues for your kernel version |

## Pain Points

- **ENOSPC due to metadata/data imbalance**: The most common Btrfs "gotcha". Btrfs allocates space in chunks — if metadata chunks fill up, writes fail even when data chunks are available and `df` still shows free space. Fix: `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to reclaim partially-empty chunks. This is not a bug — it is the expected behavior when chunk allocation becomes imbalanced.
- **Mixed RAID profiles between data and metadata**: Adding a second disk does not automatically mirror metadata. A system can have `RAID1` data but `single` metadata, meaning metadata loss on one disk is fatal. Always explicitly set both with `-d` and `-m` flags.
- **Snapshots are instant but they accumulate**: Snapshot creation is O(1) and free. Deletion requires reference counting and can be slow. Unreferenced snapshots hold on to deleted data indefinitely — disk usage only decreases after snapshot deletion completes.
- **`btrfs check` is slow and `--repair` is risky**: Unlike `fsck.ext4`, Btrfs check does not have a safe repair mode. `--repair` can corrupt a filesystem that `check` reports as damaged. Prefer `btrfs rescue` subcommands (`zero-log`, `fix-device-size`) for targeted fixes.
110→- **Btrfs RAID-5/6 has known parity issues**: As of kernels through 6.x, Btrfs RAID-5 and RAID-6 have unresolved write-hole bugs. Do not use RAID-5/6 for data you care about. Use RAID-1 or RAID-10 instead.
- **Send/receive for backups**: `btrfs send` / `btrfs receive` is efficient for incremental backups using read-only snapshots as base references. Tools like `snapper` and `btrbk` automate the snapshot lifecycle and send/receive workflow — prefer them over manual scripting.
- **CoW fragmentation on databases and VMs**: Copy-on-write writes new data to new locations, which fragments sequential files over time. Use `nodatacow` mount option (or `chattr +C`) for VM disk images, database files, and other large randomly-written files. `nodatacow` also disables checksums for those files.

## See Also

- **ext4** — Traditional Linux filesystem without CoW overhead; use when you need maximum compatibility and don't need snapshots
- **xfs** — High-performance filesystem for large sequential I/O; use for databases and media workloads where CoW fragmentation is a concern
- **zfs** — Full storage stack with pooling and replication; use when you need enterprise-grade checksums and send/receive without kernel version sensitivity
- **lvm** — Logical volume manager; provides snapshot and resize capabilities at the block layer beneath btrfs
120→
## References

See `references/` for:
- `btrfs-options.md` — mkfs and mount options organized by category
- `common-patterns.md` — filesystem setup, subvolume layouts, snapshots, rollback, backup, RAID, and compression
- `docs.md` — official documentation and community links

name: btrfs
description: >
  Btrfs filesystem administration: subvolumes, snapshots, rollback, balance,
  scrub, RAID profiles, compression, quotas, send/receive backups, and
  troubleshooting.
  MUST consult when installing, configuring, or troubleshooting btrfs.
triggerPhrases:
  - "btrfs"
  - "Btrfs"
  - "btrfs snapshot"
  - "btrfs subvolume"
  - "btrfs balance"
  - "btrfs scrub"
  - "copy-on-write filesystem"
  - "CoW filesystem"
  - "btrfs-progs"
  - "mkfs.btrfs"
  - "snapper"
  - "btrbk"
globs:
  - "**/fstab"
  - "**/etc/fstab"
last_verified: "unverified"
---

## Identity

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| **Type** | Kernel built-in filesystem (no loadable module needed on most distros) |
| **CLI tool** | `btrfs` (subcommands: `filesystem`, `subvolume`, `balance`, `scrub`, `device`, `quota`, `qgroup`, `check`, `defragment`, `rescue`) |
| **Distro install** | `apt install btrfs-progs` / `dnf install btrfs-progs` |
| **Create** | `mkfs.btrfs` |
| **Kernel version matters** | Significant stability improvements landed between 4.x and 6.x; older kernels have known bugs with RAID-5/6 and balance |

## Quick Start

```bash
sudo apt install btrfs-progs
sudo mkfs.btrfs -L mydata /dev/sdX1
sudo mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/mydata
btrfs filesystem show /mnt/mydata
btrfs device stats /mnt/mydata
```

## Key Operations

| Task | Command |
|------|---------|
| Show filesystems | `btrfs filesystem show` |
| Filesystem usage (detailed) | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` |
| List subvolumes | `btrfs subvolume list /mount` |
| Create subvolume | `btrfs subvolume create /mount/name` |
| Delete subvolume | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/name` |
| Create read-write snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/src /mount/dst` |
| Create read-only snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot -r /mount/src /mount/dst` |
| Rollback: delete current, rename snapshot | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/@; mv /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |
| Rollback: recreate subvolume from snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |
| Balance start (all chunks) | `btrfs balance start /mount` |
| Balance start (metadata only) | `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |
| Balance status | `btrfs balance status /mount` |
| Balance cancel | `btrfs balance cancel /mount` |
| Scrub start | `btrfs scrub start /mount` |
| Scrub status | `btrfs scrub status /mount` |
| Scrub cancel | `btrfs scrub cancel /mount` |
| Check filesystem (read-only) | `btrfs check /dev/sdX` (unmounted) |
| Defragment file or directory | `btrfs filesystem defragment -r /mount` |
| Resize (grow) | `btrfs filesystem resize max /mount` |
| Resize (shrink) | `btrfs filesystem resize -10G /mount` |
| Add device | `btrfs device add /dev/sdY /mount` |
| Remove device | `btrfs device remove /dev/sdY /mount` |
| Device read/write error stats | `btrfs device stats /mount` |
| Enable quotas | `btrfs quota enable /mount` |
| Show qgroup usage | `btrfs qgroup show -reF /mount` |

## Expected State

- `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters are `0` (any non-zero value is a read/write error)
- `btrfs scrub status /mount` → `Status: finished` with `0 errors`
- `btrfs balance status /mount` → `No balance found on '/mount'` when idle
- `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → Data and metadata ratios show reasonable allocation (metadata should not be >80% full)

## Health Checks

1. `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters `0`; any non-zero value means hardware errors, act immediately
2. `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → check both Data and Metadata sections; metadata ENOSPC is the most common silent failure
3. `btrfs scrub status /mount` → verify last scrub completed with no errors; schedule scrubs monthly via systemd timer or cron
4. `btrfs subvolume list /mount` → audit snapshot count; accumulation fills disk without appearing in normal `df` output

## Common Failures

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| `no space left on device` but `df` shows free space | Metadata chunks exhausted while data chunks exist | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — run `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to rebalance underused chunks |
| RAID-1 on data but single on metadata | Dangerous default when adding a second disk; metadata is not redundant | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — check metadata profile; run `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |
| Filesystem mounts read-only | Encountered an error it cannot self-correct | Check `dmesg | grep -i btrfs`; run `btrfs check /dev/sdX` on unmounted device to assess damage |
| Balance fails with ENOSPC mid-run | Not enough free space to relocate all chunks | Use `-dusage=<N>` filter to relocate only partially-used chunks first; free up space before retrying |
| Qgroup show reports inflated usage | Qgroups track snapshot references — shared data counted in each | Shared data is expected; use `btrfs qgroup show -reF` to see exclusive vs shared bytes |
| Snapshot accumulation fills disk | Old snapshots reference deleted data, preventing space reclaim | `btrfs subvolume list /mount | grep snapshot` — delete old snapshots with `btrfs subvolume delete` |
| `btrfs check --repair` made it worse | `--repair` is not safe for general use and can corrupt data | Never run `--repair` without consulting upstream; use `rescue` subcommands instead |
| Filesystem errors after kernel upgrade | Older on-disk format or regression | Check `dmesg`; downgrade kernel or use `btrfs rescue` tools; check known issues for your kernel version |

## Pain Points

- **ENOSPC due to metadata/data imbalance**: The most common Btrfs "gotcha". Btrfs allocates space in chunks — if metadata chunks fill up, writes fail even when data chunks are available and `df` still shows free space. Fix: `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to reclaim partially-empty chunks. This is not a bug — it is the expected behavior when chunk allocation becomes imbalanced.
- **Mixed RAID profiles between data and metadata**: Adding a second disk does not automatically mirror metadata. A system can have `RAID1` data but `single` metadata, meaning metadata loss on one disk is fatal. Always explicitly set both with `-d` and `-m` flags.
- **Snapshots are instant but they accumulate**: Snapshot creation is O(1) and free. Deletion requires reference counting and can be slow. Unreferenced snapshots hold on to deleted data indefinitely — disk usage only decreases after snapshot deletion completes.
- **`btrfs check` is slow and `--repair` is risky**: Unlike `fsck.ext4`, Btrfs check does not have a safe repair mode. `--repair` can corrupt a filesystem that `check` reports as damaged. Prefer `btrfs rescue` subcommands (`zero-log`, `fix-device-size`) for targeted fixes.
- **Btrfs RAID-5/6 has known parity issues**: As of kernels through 6.x, Btrfs RAID-5 and RAID-6 have unresolved write-hole bugs. Do not use RAID-5/6 for data you care about. Use RAID-1 or RAID-10 instead.
- **Send/receive for backups**: `btrfs send` / `btrfs receive` is efficient for incremental backups using read-only snapshots as base references. Tools like `snapper` and `btrbk` automate the snapshot lifecycle and send/receive workflow — prefer them over manual scripting.
- **CoW fragmentation on databases and VMs**: Copy-on-write writes new data to new locations, which fragments sequential files over time. Use `nodatacow` mount option (or `chattr +C`) for VM disk images, database files, and other large randomly-written files. `nodatacow` also disables checksums for those files.

## See Also

- **xfs** — High-performance filesystem for large sequential I/O; use for databases and media workloads where CoW fragmentation is a concern
- **zfs** — Full storage stack with pooling and replication; use when you need enterprise-grade checksums and send/receive without kernel version sensitivity
- **lvm** — Logical volume manager; provides snapshot and resize capabilities at the block layer beneath btrfs

See `references/` for:
- `btrfs-options.md` — mkfs and mount options organized by category
- `common-patterns.md` — filesystem setup, subvolume layouts, snapshots, rollback, backup, RAID, and compression
- `docs.md` — official documentation and community links

10→
# Security

Security is built-in, not bolted-on. Every feature, endpoint, and data flow must consider security implications.

## OWASP Top 10 (2025)

| #   | Vulnerability                      | Prevention                                      |
| --- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | Broken Access Control              | Verify permissions server-side, default deny    |
20→| 2   | Security Misconfiguration          | Secure defaults, remove unused features         |
| 3   | Software Supply Chain Failures     | SBOM, dependency scanning, signed builds        |
| 4   | Cryptographic Failures             | Use TLS, hash passwords (argon2id), encrypt PII |
| 5   | Injection                          | Parameterized queries, input validation         |
| 6   | Insecure Design                    | Threat modeling, security requirements          |
| 7   | Authentication Failures            | Strong passwords, MFA, secure session mgmt      |
| 8   | Software or Data Integrity         | Verify dependencies, sign releases              |
| 9   | Logging and Alerting Failures      | Log security events, set up alerts              |
| 10  | Mishandling Exceptional Conditions | Fail securely, generic errors to clients        |

30→## Security Principles

| Principle          | Rule                                                      |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Defense in Depth   | Multiple layers: firewall, auth, authz, encryption, audit |
| Least Privilege    | Minimum permissions needed, nothing more                  |
| Zero Trust         | Never trust, always verify. Assume breach.                |
| Secure by Default  | HTTPS, strict passwords, secure cookies out of the box    |
| Fail Securely      | Access denied on error, no internal details to users      |
| Validate on Server | Client validation is UX, server validation is security    |
40→
## Pre-Deployment Checklist

| Area          | Requirements                                                        |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Passwords     | Hashed with argon2id (preferred) or bcrypt (12+ rounds)             |
| Tokens        | JWT with EdDSA/ES256, 15min access / 7d refresh, httpOnly cookies   |
| Sessions      | HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies                           |
| Rate Limiting | Auth endpoints: 5 attempts/15min                                    |
| Authorization | All routes check auth server-side, default deny                     |
50→| Input         | Validated with schema (Zod), parameterized SQL                      |
| Uploads       | Whitelist types, enforce size limits                                |
| Secrets       | No secrets in code or VCS                                           |
| Headers       | CSP (with nonces), HSTS, Permissions-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options |
| CORS          | Configured restrictively                                            |
| Encryption    | PII encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.3)            |
| Logging       | Audit logging for security events                                   |
| Dependencies  | SBOM generated, `npm audit` clean, Dependabot enabled               |

## Threat Modeling (STRIDE)
60→
| Threat                 | Category        | Key Mitigations                                        |
| ---------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Spoofing               | Authentication  | MFA, strong passwords, JWT with short expiry           |
| Tampering              | Integrity       | Input validation, HTTPS/TLS, signed tokens             |
| Repudiation            | Accountability  | Audit logging, digital signatures                      |
| Info Disclosure        | Confidentiality | Encryption, least privilege, secret management         |
| Denial of Service      | Availability    | Rate limiting, input validation, CDN/DDoS protection   |
| Elevation of Privilege | Authorization   | Authz checks on every request, ABAC, permission audits |

70→## Risk Levels

| Level    | Action                    |
| -------- | ------------------------- |
| Critical | Immediate action required |
| High     | Address before launch     |
| Medium   | Address post-launch       |
| Low      | Monitor, may accept risk  |

## Compliance Overview
80→
| Framework | Scope              | Key Requirements                                                   |
| --------- | ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| GDPR      | EU data subjects   | Consent, data subject rights, breach notification (72h), DPIA      |
| HIPAA     | US healthcare data | PHI encryption, RBAC, audit logs, BAA with providers               |
| SOC 2     | SaaS customer data | Security policies, MFA, encryption, incident response              |
| PCI-DSS   | Credit card data   | Use payment processor (Stripe), tokenization, network segmentation |

## Anti-Patterns

90→| Anti-Pattern                                  | Fix                                              |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Security as afterthought                      | Integrate from design phase                      |
| Client-side authorization                     | Always verify permissions server-side            |
| Trusting client data (e.g., userId from body) | Get user ID from authenticated session           |
| Rolling your own crypto                       | Use proven libraries (argon2, bcrypt, libsodium) |
| Compliance = security                         | Compliance is the minimum; security is ongoing   |
| Verbose error responses                       | Generic messages to clients, details server-side |

## Common Mistakes
100→
| Mistake                                                       | Correct Pattern                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Performing authorization checks only on the client side       | Always verify permissions server-side; client checks are UX only    |
| Trusting user-supplied IDs from request body (e.g., userId)   | Derive user identity from the authenticated session or token        |
| Rolling custom cryptography instead of using proven libraries | Use argon2id, bcrypt, or libsodium for all cryptographic operations |
| Treating compliance certification as equivalent to security   | Compliance is the minimum bar; security requires ongoing review     |
| Returning verbose error messages with stack traces to clients | Show generic messages to clients; log details server-side only      |

## Delegation
110→
- **Scan codebase for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities and insecure patterns**: Use `Explore` agent to search for SQL injection, XSS, and hardcoded secrets
- **Implement authentication, authorization, and security headers end-to-end**: Use `Task` agent to configure JWT, RBAC, CSP, HSTS, and rate limiting
- **Design a threat model and security architecture for new features**: Use `Plan` agent to apply STRIDE methodology and map trust boundaries

> For database-layer security (RLS policies, Postgres/Supabase hardening, audit trails), use the `database-security` skill. For AI/LLM security (prompt injection defense, agentic zero-trust, MCP tool hardening), use the `secure-ai` skill.

## References

- [Threat Modeling](references/threat-modeling.md) — STRIDE methodology, risk assessment process, trust boundaries
120→- [Authentication and Authorization](references/auth.md) — JWT, session-based, OAuth, RBAC, ABAC, IDOR protection
- [API Security](references/api-security.md) — OWASP API Security Top 10, object-level authorization, rate limiting, SSRF prevention, security testing
- [Input Validation](references/input-validation.md) — SQL injection, XSS, command injection, path traversal, Zod validation, file upload security
- [Data Protection](references/data-protection.md) — Password hashing (argon2id/bcrypt), AES-256-GCM encryption, secrets management
- [Secure Configuration](references/secure-config.md) — Security headers, CORS, Express hardening, rate limiting
- [Supply Chain Security](references/supply-chain.md) — SBOM generation, dependency scanning, CI/CD hardening, artifact signing
- [Monitoring and Compliance](references/monitoring-compliance.md) — Audit logging, error handling, GDPR/HIPAA/SOC2/PCI-DSS, troubleshooting

| Principle          | Rule                                                      |

# Rust

## Overview

Rust is a systems programming language focused on safety, concurrency, and performance. The ownership system guarantees memory safety without garbage collection, and the type system enforces thread safety at compile time.
20→
**When to use:** Systems programming, web services (axum), CLI tools (clap), terminal UIs (ratatui), WebAssembly, performance-critical applications, anything requiring memory safety without runtime overhead.

**When NOT to use:** Rapid prototyping where compile times matter more than safety, simple scripting tasks, projects where the team has no Rust experience and deadlines are tight.

## Quick Reference

| Pattern             | API / Tool                          | Key Points                           |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Ownership transfer  | `let b = a;`                        | `a` is moved, no longer usable       |
30→| Borrowing           | `&T` / `&mut T`                     | One mutable OR many immutable refs   |
| Lifetime annotation | `fn f<'a>(x: &'a str) -> &'a str`   | Ties output lifetime to input        |
| Error propagation   | `?` operator                        | Converts and propagates errors       |
| Custom errors       | `thiserror::Error` derive           | Structured error types with Display  |
| Ad-hoc errors       | `anyhow::Result<T>`                 | Context chaining for applications    |
| Async runtime       | `#[tokio::main]`                    | Entry point for async programs       |
| Spawn task          | `tokio::spawn(async { })`           | Concurrent async task execution      |
| HTTP router         | `axum::Router::new().route(...)`    | Composable routing with extractors   |
| Extractors          | `Json<T>`, `Path<T>`, `State<T>`    | Type-safe request parsing            |
| Serialization       | `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` | serde with format-agnostic derives   |
40→| CLI parsing         | `#[derive(Parser)]`                 | clap derive API for arg parsing      |
| TUI rendering       | `terminal.draw(\|f\| { })`          | Immediate-mode ratatui rendering     |
| Benchmarking        | `criterion::Criterion`              | Statistical benchmarking framework   |
| Dep auditing        | `cargo deny check`                  | License, vulnerability, source audit |
| Binary release      | `cargo dist init`                   | Cross-platform binary distribution   |
| Changelog           | `release-plz update`                | Auto semver bump and changelog       |

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                 | Correct Pattern                               |
50→| --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Returning reference to local variable   | Return owned type or use lifetime parameter   |
| Using `unwrap()` in library code        | Return `Result` and let caller decide         |
| `clone()` to satisfy borrow checker     | Restructure code to avoid the borrow conflict |
| Blocking in async context               | Use `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`             |
| Shared mutable state without sync       | Use `Arc<Mutex<T>>` or channels               |
| `String` where `&str` suffices          | Accept `&str` in function parameters          |
| Ignoring `must_use` warnings            | Handle or explicitly discard with `let _ =`   |
| Large enum variants                     | Box the large variant to reduce overall size  |
| `async fn` in traits without bounds     | Add `Send` bound or use `async-trait` crate   |
60→| Missing `#[tokio::test]` on async tests | Use `#[tokio::test]` instead of `#[test]`     |

## Delegation

- **Code exploration**: Use `Explore` agent
- **Architecture review**: Use `Task` agent
- **Code review**: Delegate to `code-reviewer` agent

> If the `docker` skill is available, delegate multi-stage container build patterns to it.
> If the `github-actions` skill is available, delegate CI pipeline configuration to it.
70→> If the `openapi` skill is available, delegate API specification and code generation to it.

| Error propagation   | `?` operator                        | Converts and propagates errors       |
| Custom errors       | `thiserror::Error` derive           | Structured error types with Display  |
| Ad-hoc errors       | `anyhow::Result<T>`                 | Context chaining for applications    |
| Async runtime       | `#[tokio::main]`                    | Entry point for async programs       |
| Spawn task          | `tokio::spawn(async { })`           | Concurrent async task execution      |
| HTTP router         | `axum::Router::new().route(...)`    | Composable routing with extractors   |
| Extractors          | `Json<T>`, `Path<T>`, `State<T>`    | Type-safe request parsing            |
| Serialization       | `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` | serde with format-agnostic derives   |
| CLI parsing         | `#[derive(Parser)]`                 | clap derive API for arg parsing      |
| TUI rendering       | `terminal.draw(\|f\| { })`          | Immediate-mode ratatui rendering     |
| Benchmarking        | `criterion::Criterion`              | Statistical benchmarking framework   |
| Dep auditing        | `cargo deny check`                  | License, vulnerability, source audit |
| Binary release      | `cargo dist init`                   | Cross-platform binary distribution   |
| Changelog           | `release-plz update`                | Auto semver bump and changelog       |

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                                 | Correct Pattern                               |
| --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Returning reference to local variable   | Return owned type or use lifetime parameter   |
| Using `unwrap()` in library code        | Return `Result` and let caller decide         |
| `clone()` to satisfy borrow checker     | Restructure code to avoid the borrow conflict |
| Blocking in async context               | Use `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`             |
| Shared mutable state without sync       | Use `Arc<Mutex<T>>` or channels               |
| `String` where `&str` suffices          | Accept `&str` in function parameters          |
| Ignoring `must_use` warnings            | Handle or explicitly discard with `let _ =`   |
| Large enum variants                     | Box the large variant to reduce overall size  |
| `async fn` in traits without bounds     | Add `Send` bound or use `async-trait` crate   |
| Missing `#[tokio::test]` on async tests | Use `#[tokio::test]` instead of `#[test]`     |

## Delegation

- **Code exploration**: Use `Explore` agent
- **Architecture review**: Use `Task` agent
- **Code review**: Delegate to `code-reviewer` agent

> If the `docker` skill is available, delegate multi-stage container build patterns to it.
> If the `github-actions` skill is available, delegate CI pipeline configuration to it.
> If the `openapi` skill is available, delegate API specification and code generation to it.

## References

- [Ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, and type system patterns](references/ownership-and-types.md)
- [Error handling with Result, Option, thiserror, and anyhow](references/error-handling.md)
- [Async programming with Tokio runtime and concurrency](references/async-tokio.md)
- [Web APIs and backends with axum, tower, and sqlx](references/axum-web.md)
- [Terminal user interfaces with ratatui and crossterm](references/ratatui-tui.md)
- [CLI applications with clap, config, and signal handling](references/cli-applications.md)
- [Testing patterns and criterion benchmarking](references/testing-and-benchmarks.md)
- [Release pipeline with cargo-deny, cargo-dist, and release-plz](references/release-pipeline.md)

description: Use when starting any conversation - establishes how to find and use skills, requiring skill invocation before ANY response including clarifying questions
---

<SUBAGENT-STOP>
If you were dispatched as a subagent to execute a specific task, ignore this skill.
</SUBAGENT-STOP>

10→<EXTREMELY-IMPORTANT>
If you think there is even a 1% chance a skill might apply to what you are doing, you ABSOLUTELY MUST invoke the skill.

IF A SKILL APPLIES TO YOUR TASK, YOU DO NOT HAVE A CHOICE. YOU MUST USE IT.

This is not negotiable. You cannot rationalize your way out of this.
</EXTREMELY-IMPORTANT>

## The Rule

20→**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

Then announce "Using [skill] to [purpose]" and follow the skill exactly. If it has a checklist, create a todo per item.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

30→- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
40→| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
50→| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

1→---
name: typesafe-ai
license: MIT
description: >
  TypeSafe integration craft for System One models (sometimes called Decision Models) such as Jev,
  which answer typed questions about text, images, and application state with calibrated
  probabilities. Use when building, reviewing, or debugging code that calls TypeSafe; when writing
  its questions or state; when replacing an LLM prompt-and-parse step, keyword matching, or a
  brittle heuristic with a typed question; or when brainstorming where programmable common sense
10→  fits in an app.
---

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe's **Jev**, the first public **System One model**, answers typed questions about state your
application supplies. State is the text, images, and application data your code sends with a
request. Jev can answer a Choice among options, a Noul (the probability that a statement is true), a
Score on levels you describe, or a Box that locates something in an image. Each answer comes back as
typed data with calibrated probabilities, for your code to use.
20→
The rest of this skill is guidance: patterns that tend to produce reliable integrations. None of it
is absolute. Models change, applications differ, and edge cases exist. When a situation calls for
something else, test the alternative and use your judgment.

## Judgments from Jev, decisions in code

Integrations tend to work best when Jev makes the judgments and code decides what to do with
them. Think of each decision as a **truth table**. Jev supplies the inputs, such as "Does the
customer sound frustrated?" or "Which product is the message about?". Code holds the logic that
30→maps those inputs to an action.

A question that asks Jev to make the decision, such as "Should this ticket be escalated?" or "What
should the agent do next?", usually means the question is at the wrong layer. Instead, break the
decision into the judgments it depends on, and write the decision itself in code, where it's
visible and testable. Writing out the table often shows gaps in the business logic too. A
combination of judgments with no defined outcome is a design question about the system, and it is
best settled in code.

## Live docs
40→
The live docs are the source of truth for request syntax, SDKs, question types, limits, and current
model behavior. Read the relevant pages as part of the task.

- Start at the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt). Append `.md` to a page
  path to get the page as Markdown, and resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Exact request and response schemas: the [OpenAPI spec](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) and
  the [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/api.md) page. For an SDK, see the
  [Python](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/python-sdk.md) or
  [JavaScript](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk.md) page and the types in the installed package.
50→- Question types: [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/primitives.md) and each type's own page,
  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).
- Models, context limits, and rate limits: [models](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/models.md). Known
  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the
  [jaggedness page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/jaggedness.md).
- Architecture: [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/how-to-build.md),
  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.
60→
If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
70→   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
80→   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
90→in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
100→  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.
110→
## Write the questions

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions
about what might make something fraud or spam. Each question tends to work best when it asks for
**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

- **Ask the concrete, observable thing.** Aim for something a person could point to: "Is a SQL
120→  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".
- **One judgment per question; beware the "or".** Two conditions joined by "or" or "and" usually
  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.
- **Anchor intent to the goal.** When the judgment is about what someone wants, it helps to name
  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".
- **Name the subject directly.** "Where is the coffee mug in `photo`?" reads better than "Where is
  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
130→  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context
  that many questions share can go in the state once, and each question can refer to it by its
  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.
- **Each question is answered on its own.** Questions in a request can't see each other or each
  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and
  output-format instructions add noise. Descriptions of the options belong in the criteria, not in
  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
140→  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".
- **Name the case that causes confusion.** If answers keep mixing up two outcomes, say in the
  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

### Criteria

- **Ask about the null case separately.** A Box always returns a location and a Choice always picks
  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
150→  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our
  products?"), so code can tell when nothing does. As of Jev 1.14, this companion Noul usually works
  better than a "none of the above" option.
- **Option names are sent to the model; question IDs are not.** Names that describe the content
  (`refund_request`, `shipping_delay`) help the model. Positional names (`A`, `left`, `option_1`)
  give it nothing meaningful to go on and can bias the answer.
- **Keep options distinct and concrete.** Wording that options share with each other, or with the
  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
160→  mixed into the other.
- **Describe each Score level as a situation.** Each level should make sense when read on its own:
  "The customer mentions a minor inconvenience" rather than "More upset than the previous level".
- **Describe a Noul's `false` criterion as a concrete situation**, such as "the package arrived on
  time", rather than as "not late".
- **Use a Noul per statement when more than one can be true.** A Choice picks one option, so a
  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

## Compose requests
170→
**Bundle questions that share state.** A handy heuristic: if two calls would send the same state
with different questions, they can likely be one call. Questions are cheap and run in parallel, and
the state is read and paid for once. See
[parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md).

**Ask speculatively**, meaning ask a question before you know whether you'll need its answer. A
question that only matters in some cases can go in the same request as the question that
identifies the case. Ask "Is `order` a return request?" and "Which item in `order.items` is being
returned?" together, and have code read the second answer only when the first is yes. The second
180→question doesn't need an "if" clause, because code handles the condition. See
[speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).

A second request is usually worth it when:

- code needs an answer to build the next state, fetch evidence, or choose the next options;
- a state field needed for one question measurably misleads another;
- different sets of questions need to be cached or versioned separately.

## Read the answers
190→
### Confidence is rarely the gate

Naive implementations often use an answer's `confidence` as the check that decides whether code
acts. Confidence measures how concentrated an answer's probability distribution is, which is not
the same as how likely the answer is to be correct. Think about what the probabilities should look
like in your use case; another calculation over them may suit it better.

### Probabilities and thresholds

200→- **A probability is the likelihood that an answer is correct.** Jev isn't a calculator for
  probability problems. Ask it for judgments, and do any math on odds or probabilities in code. A
  Noul near 0.5 usually means the state doesn't settle the question.
- **The top answer is a good default**: the Choice's top option, or the Score's position.
- **0.7 and 0.3 make good starting thresholds for a Noul**: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no,
  and the band between means the question isn't settled, which can get its own row in the truth

name: typesafe-ai
license: MIT
description: >

  which answer typed questions about text, images, and application state with calibrated
  probabilities. Use when building, reviewing, or debugging code that calls TypeSafe; when writing
  its questions or state; when replacing an LLM prompt-and-parse step, keyword matching, or a
  brittle heuristic with a typed question; or when brainstorming where programmable common sense
10→  fits in an app.

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe's **Jev**, the first public **System One model**, answers typed questions about state your
application supplies. State is the text, images, and application data your code sends with a
request. Jev can answer a Choice among options, a Noul (the probability that a statement is true), a
Score on levels you describe, or a Box that locates something in an image. Each answer comes back as
typed data with calibrated probabilities, for your code to use.
20→
The rest of this skill is guidance: patterns that tend to produce reliable integrations. None of it
is absolute. Models change, applications differ, and edge cases exist. When a situation calls for
something else, test the alternative and use your judgment.

## Judgments from Jev, decisions in code

Integrations tend to work best when Jev makes the judgments and code decides what to do with
them. Think of each decision as a **truth table**. Jev supplies the inputs, such as "Does the
customer sound frustrated?" or "Which product is the message about?". Code holds the logic that
30→maps those inputs to an action.

A question that asks Jev to make the decision, such as "Should this ticket be escalated?" or "What
should the agent do next?", usually means the question is at the wrong layer. Instead, break the
decision into the judgments it depends on, and write the decision itself in code, where it's
visible and testable. Writing out the table often shows gaps in the business logic too. A
combination of judgments with no defined outcome is a design question about the system, and it is
best settled in code.

## Live docs
40→
The live docs are the source of truth for request syntax, SDKs, question types, limits, and current
model behavior. Read the relevant pages as part of the task.

- Start at the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt). Append `.md` to a page
  path to get the page as Markdown, and resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Exact request and response schemas: the [OpenAPI spec](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) and
  the [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/api.md) page. For an SDK, see the
  [Python](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/python-sdk.md) or
  [JavaScript](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk.md) page and the types in the installed package.
50→- Question types: [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/primitives.md) and each type's own page,
  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).
- Models, context limits, and rate limits: [models](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/models.md). Known
  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the
  [jaggedness page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/jaggedness.md).
- Architecture: [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/how-to-build.md),
  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.
60→
If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
70→   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
80→   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
90→in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
100→  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.
110→

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions

**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

120→  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".

  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.

  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".

  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
130→  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context
  that many questions share can go in the state once, and each question can refer to it by its
  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.

  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and
  output-format instructions add noise. Descriptions of the options belong in the criteria, not in
  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
140→  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".
- **Name the case that causes confusion.** If answers keep mixing up two outcomes, say in the
  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

### Criteria

- **Ask about the null case separately.** A Box always returns a location and a Choice always picks
  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
150→  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our
  products?"), so code can tell when nothing does. As of Jev 1.14, this companion Noul usually works
  better than a "none of the above" option.
- **Option names are sent to the model; question IDs are not.** Names that describe the content
  (`refund_request`, `shipping_delay`) help the model. Positional names (`A`, `left`, `option_1`)
  give it nothing meaningful to go on and can bias the answer.
- **Keep options distinct and concrete.** Wording that options share with each other, or with the
  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
160→  mixed into the other.
- **Describe each Score level as a situation.** Each level should make sense when read on its own:
  "The customer mentions a minor inconvenience" rather than "More upset than the previous level".
- **Describe a Noul's `false` criterion as a concrete situation**, such as "the package arrived on
  time", rather than as "not late".
- **Use a Noul per statement when more than one can be true.** A Choice picks one option, so a
  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

170→

with different questions, they can likely be one call. Questions are cheap and run in parallel, and
the state is read and paid for once. See
[parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md).

identifies the case. Ask "Is `order` a return request?" and "Which item in `order.items` is being

180→question doesn't need an "if" clause, because code handles the condition. See

application supplies. State is the text, images, and application data your code sends with a

  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).

  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the

1→---
name: incus
description: >
  Incus system containers and VMs: instance/profile YAML, disk devices,
  native storage pools and volumes, Btrfs subvolumes, lifecycle and isolation.
  Consult before creating or changing an Incus instance, profile, disk,
  storage volume, root binding or provisioning helper.
triggerPhrases:
  - "Incus"
10→  - "Incus disk"
  - "Incus profile"
  - "Incus storage"
  - "container root disk"
  - "native storage volume"
last_verified: "2026-10-19"
---

# Incus: configuration first, storage-driver ownership

20→Project-local skill authored from the official Incus documentation below;
not an imported third-party skill or a container-sandbox wrapper. Documentation
review is not proof that any example has been applied to this host. Check the
installed client/server version and applicable API extensions before using
version-dependent options.

## Start with the actual declaration

An Incus instance is configured through instance properties, `config`,
`devices` and ordered `profiles`. The CLI exposes this as YAML; do not invent
30→a separate authoritative YAML file on disk. Incus owns its configuration.

Read both local and expanded instance configuration. Later profiles override
earlier ones; instance-local configuration overrides profiles. Editing a
shared profile affects every instance that uses it. Do not use expanded
configuration as a blind replacement: it flattens inherited settings.

Read-only infrastructure diagnostics, within the assigned maintenance scope:

```sh
40→incus version
incus config show <instance>
incus config show <instance> --expanded
incus profile show <profile>
incus storage show <pool>
incus storage volume list <pool>
incus storage volume show <pool> container/<instance>
```

Confirm the selected remote, project, instance type, native UUID and stopped
50→or running state. A name alone is not an identity or authorization proof.
Use `--force-local` only when explicitly diagnosing this host's local daemon.

## Declare native disks under devices

Example fragment for a NEW container's root on an existing Btrfs pool named
`3tched` (not a migration instruction for an existing container):

```yaml
devices:
60→  root:
    type: disk
    pool: 3tched
    path: /
```

Incus creates the instance's root storage volume at instance creation. Its
Btrfs driver uses a subvolume for a container filesystem volume. Do not
manually create a per-container `.img`, GPT, `losetup` mapping or filesystem
as an assumed prerequisite for this native root declaration.
70→
Additional managed filesystem volumes are separate objects. Create the
custom volume through the supported control plane first; its device then
names the pool, volume and guest mount path:

```yaml
devices:
  data:
    type: disk
    pool: 3tched
```

# Incus: configuration first, storage-driver ownership

Project-local skill authored from the official Incus documentation below;
not an imported third-party skill or a container-sandbox wrapper. Documentation
review is not proof that any example has been applied to this host. Check the
installed client/server version and applicable API extensions before using
version-dependent options.

## Start with the actual declaration

An Incus instance is configured through instance properties, `config`,
`devices` and ordered `profiles`. The CLI exposes this as YAML; do not invent
a separate authoritative YAML file on disk. Incus owns its configuration.

Read both local and expanded instance configuration. Later profiles override
earlier ones; instance-local configuration overrides profiles. Editing a
shared profile affects every instance that uses it. Do not use expanded
configuration as a blind replacement: it flattens inherited settings.

Read-only infrastructure diagnostics, within the assigned maintenance scope:

```sh
incus version
incus config show <instance>
incus config show <instance> --expanded
incus profile show <profile>
incus storage show <pool>
incus storage volume list <pool>
incus storage volume show <pool> container/<instance>
```

Confirm the selected remote, project, instance type, native UUID and stopped
or running state. A name alone is not an identity or authorization proof.
Use `--force-local` only when explicitly diagnosing this host's local daemon.

## Declare native disks under devices

Example fragment for a NEW container's root on an existing Btrfs pool named
`3tched` (not a migration instruction for an existing container):

```yaml
devices:
  root:
    type: disk
    pool: 3tched
    path: /
```

Incus creates the instance's root storage volume at instance creation. Its
Btrfs driver uses a subvolume for a container filesystem volume. Do not
manually create a per-container `.img`, GPT, `losetup` mapping or filesystem
as an assumed prerequisite for this native root declaration.

Additional managed filesystem volumes are separate objects. Create the
custom volume through the supported control plane first; its device then
names the pool, volume and guest mount path:

```yaml
devices:
  data:
    type: disk
    pool: 3tched
    source: identity-data
    path: /data
```

This references an existing custom filesystem volume named `identity-data`;
it does not create that volume. Custom volumes persist independently of the
instance until explicitly deleted. Do not casually share identity-private
volumes. A device with a host-path `source` and no pool is a host-backed
mount, not an Incus-managed custom volume.

For standalone Incus administration, the native commands are
`incus storage volume create <pool> <volume>` (filesystem by default),
`incus storage volume attach <pool> <volume> <instance> <device> <guest-path>`
and `incus config device add <instance> <device> disk pool=<pool> source=<volume> path=<guest-path>`.
These are reference syntax, NOT permission to bypass this repository's
identity-bound provisioning operations. Do not replay them against an
already provisioned identity without the authorized maintenance contract.

## Do not conflate these layers

| Object | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Btrfs pool backing | Existing block device, loop file or Btrfs subvolume; inspect the pool's `source`. |
| Container filesystem volume | Managed filesystem tree; Btrfs driver represents it as a subvolume. No additional loop per volume is needed. |
| Container `type: disk` device | Mount inside the container, not a VM-style emulated partitioned disk. A host block source is mounted, not automatically passed through as guest block hardware. |
| Custom `block` or `iso` volume | Attachable to VMs, not containers. Do not switch instance type to work around this restriction. |
| Btrfs VM disk | Incus uses a backing file because Btrfs does not natively provide block volumes. This is not the container-volume model. |
| Btrfs seeding/sprouting | Separate block-device filesystem operation; a subvolume is not a writable block member for `btrfs device add`. |

A loop backing an entire existing Incus pool does not imply a loop for each
container. Never detach an existing pool backing to satisfy a statement that
container subvolumes need no loops. Do not create new loop-backed pools or
per-container raw images unless that distinct layout is explicitly requested.

An Incus root declaration alone does NOT implement an external immutable
seed plus writable Btrfs member, a GPT two-partition upgrade replica, or a
read-only overlay. Name any conflict between such requirements and native
filesystem volumes before changing the design. Do not silently replace
seeding with copied roots, snapshots, or an OverlayFS provisioning fallback.
Use the `btrfs` skill for actual seed, membership and send/receive mechanics;
Incus owns its managed-volume lifecycle.

## Preserve ownership, lifecycle and admission

- Begin repository operations in the assigned identity's mounted 3tchedFS.
  Discover declared operations and arguments there. Preserve principal,
  session, grants and Cozo identity-to-storage binding. Missing admission is
  not permission to use the local Incus socket or edit Cozo directly.
- Inspect current native configuration and the provisioning owner before
  changing an existing root. Changing the `pool` key is not a storage migration.
  Preserve native UUID, session/key binding, mount ownership and receipts.
- Keep containers unprivileged, their UID/GID mapping, storage ioctl denials
  and existing device allowlist. Do not grant guest block administration,
  nesting, unrestricted host paths or daemon sockets to make storage work.
- Explicit creation may establish approved storage once. Login, boot, start,
  stop, restart, logout and recovery must not allocate new identity leaves
  or add/remove Btrfs members. Restore/verify existing storage instead.
- Do not mutate Incus-owned storage directories or live overlay lower layers
  behind the daemon. Host storage maintenance must use its supported owner,
  exact device/FSID/mount checks and explicit authorized scope.
- Before any receive, verify the intended mounted destination and its FSID;
  an existing directory is insufficient. Never receive into a fallback path
  on the host root filesystem when the intended mount is missing.
- Distinguish source configuration, accepted operation, native state and
  deployed readiness. Report the operation receipt and authoritative result;
  no claim of success from writing YAML alone. Do not auto-start containers,
  change service managers or run test suites merely to install this skill.

## 3tched Ubuntu provisioning contract

- Use Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (Resolute Raccoon) inside the container. This does not
  change the host's distribution or service manager.
- Reuse the initialized 3tched Ubuntu seed contents, including when the owner
  explicitly selects different backing storage. A generic Ubuntu root archive
  may initialize a new seed only; never use a generic image as a later
  container-root fallback. Never modify a sealed seed with retained dependents.
- Compose each root from that seed through the existing host storage owner.
  Preserve existing 3tched integrations and network declarations; install only
  demonstrated container runtime dependencies.
- Keep persistent CozoDB data on the approved identity-owned writable storage.
  Do not force a separate Cozo subvolume through `btrfs device add`: that
  operation applies only when the selected design actually adds a block member.
  An Incus filesystem subvolume is not a block-device operand. Require the
  exact approved device before adding it; do not infer permission to allocate
  a raw image, loop, LV or replacement disk.
- For an explicitly approved partitioned seed image, a host `losetup
  --find --show --partscan IMAGE` mapping exposes partition devices such as
  `/dev/loopNp1` and `/dev/loopNp2`; separate loop allocations per partition
  are not inherently required. Finalize and unmount the root filesystem before
  setting `btrfstune -S 1` on partition 1 only. Check the existing SEEDING flag
  and skip an already sealed base; never retune on login/start/reboot. The flag
  persists in the image, while kernel mappings must be restored after reboot.
  Protect only the base partition read-only, not the whole image when partition
  2 must remain writable. Never set SEEDING on the upgrade receive filesystem.
- Distinguish an immutable base partition from a writable upgrade receiver.
  Keep the receiver filesystem/parent writable for `btrfs receive`, while
  preserving received snapshots and common incremental baselines read-only.
  Receive a new version into the parent, not over an existing `@upgrade`;
  publish it only through the host-owned overlay lifecycle, without modifying
  an in-use lower tree. Track each container's receiver and baseline explicitly;
  do not infer a shared mutable receiver from a shared image/template name.
- When the owner explicitly requests a raw leaf image under the Cozo store,
  first locate the live store through supported metadata or open-path evidence;
  do not create a duplicate database or read private records to find its path.
  Put image files outside RocksDB `data`, use a private directory and exclusive
  creation, and retain the exact size/inode/operation result. A created image
  does not establish Btrfs membership or migrate Cozo data into that image.
- Distinguish direct regular-file rejection from a provisioning-policy denial.
  Installed btrfs-progs may reject a regular `.img` with `is not a block device`;
  report that real result rather than claiming completion or silently creating
  a loop/device-mapper alternative against the owner's instruction. Full
  allocation does not change a regular file's type: if a nonsparse retry is
  explicitly requested, verify allocated bytes (disable compression on the
  empty file before writing zeros), and do not repeat that allocation after
  the same type rejection.
- Reconcile matching creation receipts and verify the retained storage binding
  on repeats. Normal lifecycle operations must not repeat device-add, format
  storage or recreate roots. Interrupted intent requires reconciliation, not
  an automatic new allocation.
- Reuse existing identity, authorization and policy services. Do not build
  parallel services, mint new credentials, broaden grants or edit Cozo
  directly as part of OS provisioning. Verify the mounted filesystem and
  authoritative binding before claiming persistence is configured.

## Official references

Consult the version matching the installed daemon where behavior differs.
These upstream pages were reviewed for this skill on 2026-10-19:

- [Instance configuration](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/explanation/instance_config/)
- [Profiles and inheritance](https://linuxcontainers.org/incus/docs/main/profiles/)

1→# JEV schema judgments
When JEV may rename tched to threetched, and 2026-10-26 crate-scan counts and scope.

## Preference

- Use JEV (TypeSafe) to judge fixes that replace leftover tched-bridge references with the captured threetched schema.
- Do not blindly rename leftover tched_router identifiers in op-grpc-bridge to threetched. tched names can be instance locators or legacy transport. Only stale hand-rolled schema references should be rewired to the pinned capture.
- Fix a judged tched defect literally line by line, not as a blind rename, and without search tools.
- If a match containing tched is not the defect, consult JEV for context and for where the code lives in zeroclaw when it is not the hand-rolled implementation.
10→- Reviewed tched hits are marked by renaming them to threetched only after JEV classifies the token. Unjudged spellings stay so addressed items stay visible.
- Rename a tched token to the threetched form only after JEV (jev-latest, noul act >= 0.7, reject <= 0.3, else abstain) classifies it as the removed hand-rolled bridge or this repo's own schema/gRPC label.
- Real ZeroClaw 0.8.4 commands stay unchanged. Do not rename environment-variable keys, D-Bus object paths, or on-disk socket paths.
- Do not ask JEV whether to rename.
- When JEV judges a tched token is the removed hand-rolled bridge or an own schema/gRPC label, edit the source in the same step.
- A receipt only logs edits that already landed. Do not stop at a receipt or invent edits when no judged defect exists.
- During the scan do not run cargo, tests, clippy, fmt, or deploy, and do not use ripgrep to hunt tched tokens.
- Per-crate reads use receipt /var/tmp/threetched-jev-20261026/<crate>/receipt.md under /srv/git/odbus-verified.
- A crate agent must not edit other crates, HANDOFF.md, SIGNALS.md, or vendor/.
- op-uds-relay is excluded from the workspace and op-ml is disabled, so neither is in the scan.
20→- On 2026-10-26 the user first narrowed the threetched review to the bridge and cache crates only, then later the same day asked JEV ("jefe") about every endpoint, method, and route referenced by tched/threetched naming, across all crates rather than only the bridge or cache.
- Inline changes should wait on a per-item JEV judgment.
- Real zeroclaw command names should not be renamed just because they appear near tched/threetched references.
- Owner-fixed threetched-fs names must not be renamed: Cargo package tched-fs, plugin tched_fs, directory crates/threetched-fs, mount /run/mounts/3tchedFS.
- Open vSwitch bridge names are not the removed tched-bridge.
- 2026-10-26 line-by-line scan of op-dbus-model (390 lines: Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs, src/models.rs, SPEC.md, compare-op-dbus-model.md) found no tched identifiers, including tched_router, tched-bridge, Tched, TCHED, 3tched, and threetched. JEV was not called and nothing was renamed. Receipt: /var/tmp/threetched-jev-20261026/op-dbus-model/receipt.md.
- 2026-10-26 scan of op-compliance (Cargo.toml 12 lines, src/lib.rs 324 lines) found no tched identifiers. JEV was not called and nothing was renamed. Scan complete. Receipt: /var/tmp/threetched-jev-20261026/op-compliance/receipt.md.
- Full line-by-line read of /srv/git/odbus-verified/crates/op-cache found no tched, tched_router, tched-bridge, Tched, TCHED, or 3tched tokens, so JEV was not called and no source edit was made. Receipt: /var/tmp/threetched-jev-20261026/op-cache/receipt.md.
- Absence of that string is not a pass if hand-rolled plugin, router, or bridge schema-cache code remains.
- Btrfs, workflow, and NUMA caches must not be renamed to threetched.
30→- Literal "threetched" in crates rs/proto/toml is concentrated in op-plugins (17), op-grpc-bridge (17), and threetched-fs (15), plus op-chat (3), op-chat-responder (2), and one file each in op-web, op-state-store, op-snowball, op-llm, op-deployment, op-cozo-store, op-cognitive, and op-blob.
- A broader token search for tched in rs/proto also hits op-cozo-store (9), op-network (4), op-mcp, op-state, op-mcp-aggregator, op-identity, op-execution-tracker, and op-agents among others. No line audit of those counts was finished.
